title: Australia's Revised General Insurance Code Would Make Insurer Promises Legally Enforceable and Auto-Accept Home and Motor Claims After 12 Months, as AFCA Reports 36,022 Complaints
summary: The Insurance Council of Australia has submitted a revised General Insurance Code of Practice to ASIC that would write its obligations into consumer contracts and automatically accept home and motor property claims left undecided for 12 months, while AFCA's 2025-26 review recorded 36,022 general insurance complaints, up 5%, with claim delays up 25% to 8,246.
description:
Australia's general insurers have put forward a stricter code of conduct, and the numbers from the industry's complaints scheme explain why. Insurance Business reported on October 22, 2026 that the Insurance Council of Australia has submitted a revised General Insurance Code of Practice to the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, which "will now review the Code for approval." Until ASIC approves it, the Code remains a proposal. The article gives no start date, and says a transition period is expected before the Code applies to new and renewed policies. It does not mention penalties.

The most significant change is legal. For the first time, the Code's obligations would be written into consumer insurance contracts, which would make them contractually enforceable. Policyholders could enforce them through the courts, through the Australian Financial Complaints Authority or through an independent Code Governance Committee. Insurance Council chief executive Andrew Hall said: "Insurance is a promise to be there when people need it most." The change responds to a 2024 House Standing Committee on Economics inquiry, "Flood failure to future fairness", which made 86 recommendations after the 2022 floods. Its chair, Dr Daniel Mulino, described "the collective failure by insurers" to meet their obligations to policyholders. The revised Code addresses the inquiry's calls for ASIC registration, contractual enforceability and automatic acceptance of claims after 12 months.

The automatic acceptance rule is the most concrete protection. Under the revised Code, home and motor vehicle property claims would be automatically accepted after 12 months if no decision had been made because of circumstances within the insurer's control. A senior employee must review any property claim at least three months before the automatic acceptance date, and the review must be completed within 20 business days. If no decision follows, the insurer must give written notice on whether the claim qualifies and what factors are causing the delay. Insurers must also decide a claim or give written reasons for delay within four months, and external experts must deliver their reports within 60 business days of appointment.

Other provisions cover vulnerable customers and settlements. Vulnerability is defined by circumstance and can affect anyone, and a new "Extra Care" framework commits insurers to tailored support and flexibility. The definition of family and domestic violence now includes financial abuse and coercion, with contractually enforceable protections, and an intervention order is not required. For home building claims, a cash settlement must be based on the insurer's reasonable calculation of the cost to the customer of completing the rebuild or repair, and customers can ask for a review within 12 months if they show the amount was insufficient. Several sections state that insurers meet their obligations by providing information to the broker, which makes brokers the conduit for compliance on the policies they place.

The National Insurance Brokers Association supports stronger consumer protections but, in a July 2026 submission described in the article, flagged limits. It noted that the policy prevails over the Code in a conflict and that exclusions apply for failures caused by events beyond the insurer's control. It asked that the broker pass-through not reduce customer protections and that brokers' own Code obligations be recognised, and it recommended shortening the four-month decision period and treating it as an outer limit.

The complaints data show why claims handling is the focus. AFCA's 2025-26 Annual Review, reported by Insurance Business the same day, recorded 36,022 general insurance complaints, up 5% on the previous year and the fifth consecutive year of growth. General insurance was AFCA's second-largest source of complaints behind banking and finance. Claim handling delays were the most common issue for the fifth year running, at 8,246 complaints, up 25%. Claim denials rose 47% to 6,561, and disputes over the amount of a claim rose 20% to 6,376. Denials based on an exclusion or condition rose from 2,503 to 3,384. Motor vehicle comprehensive was the most complained-about product, with 14,430 complaints, up 28%, and home building complaints rose 25% to 8,547 after two years of decline. Consumer credit insurance had 2,636 complaints, travel insurance 2,459 and home contents 1,756.

There was some good news on speed. AFCA closed 37,069 general insurance complaints, more than the 36,022 it received, and the average time to close fell from 96 to 84 days, with about 54% closed within 60 days. More than 15,700 closed at the referral stage and 14,143 during case management, together over 80% of closures. NIBA said broker-related complaints make up under 1% of AFCA complaints. Across all sectors AFCA received 119,949 complaints, up 19%, and awarded $834,197,535 in compensation; 41% of determinations favoured complainants and 59% favoured firms. Supply constraints in skilled trades, repair capacity and parts are lengthening motor and home repair times, according to the article.

AFCA chief ombudsman David Locke said: "Nobody wants to see this number of complaints," and that insurers remain responsible for keeping customers informed and explaining delays, while acknowledging climate and supply-chain pressures. The current Code already requires a claims decision within four months and progress updates at least every 20 business days; the revised Code would add legal force and the 12-month backstop.

What happens next depends on ASIC's review. Readers should treat the details above as the submitted proposal, since ASIC may require changes, and should look to the Insurance Council and ASIC for the final text and commencement date.
source_name: Insurance Business Australia (October 22, 2026), reporting the Insurance Council of Australia's revised Code and AFCA's 2025-26 Annual Review
image_alt: Insurance documents and pen representing a code of practice and policy contract (illustrative)
key_points: The Insurance Council of Australia has submitted a revised General Insurance Code of Practice to ASIC for approval; for the first time its obligations would be written into consumer insurance contracts, so policyholders could enforce them through the courts, AFCA or an independent Code Governance Committee.

Home and motor vehicle property claims would be automatically accepted after 12 months if no decision was made for reasons within the insurer's control, after a senior employee review at least three months before that date, completed within 20 business days.

Insurers must decide a claim or give written reasons for delay within four months, and external experts must deliver reports within 60 business days of appointment; the article gives no start date and expects a transition period.

AFCA's 2025-26 Annual Review shows 36,022 general insurance complaints, up 5% for a fifth straight year, with claim handling delays at 8,246 (up 25%), claim denials at 6,561 (up 47%), motor comprehensive at 14,430 (up 28%) and home building at 8,547 (up 25%).

A new 'Extra Care' framework commits insurers to tailored support for vulnerable customers, the family and domestic violence definition expands to include financial abuse and coercion, and cash settlements for home building claims must reflect the insurer's reasonable calculation of the cost to complete the repair.
why_it_matters: A code of practice that is only a promise can be hard to enforce; one written into the contract can be relied on by the policyholder. If ASIC approves the revised Code, claims delays that have been the top complaint for five years would carry a hard deadline, and a claim left undecided could be treated as accepted. For insurers, the changes affect claims processes, expert-report timetables and how they communicate through brokers. The Code has not yet been approved and has no start date, so the protections described are proposals, not law.

title: Intact and Definity Put Third-Quarter Catastrophe Losses at About C$850 Million Combined, Pushing Intact Above Its Annual Guidance
summary: Intact Financial estimated third-quarter 2026 catastrophe losses of about C$660 million ($2.76 per diluted share) and Definity about C$190 million ($1.15 per share), together roughly C$850 million, driven by Ontario and Alberta flooding and British Columbia wildfires, lifting Intact's trailing 12-month losses to C$1.29 billion against C$1.20 billion of annual guidance.
description:
Canada's two largest listed property and casualty insurers have given early warning that the summer's weather was costly. In separate announcements reported by Insurance Business on October 7, 2026 and Reinsurance News the following day, Intact Financial Corporation and Definity Financial Corporation estimated their third-quarter catastrophe losses at about C$850 million combined, net of reinsurance. The figures are estimates released ahead of the full quarterly results, which both companies are due to report in the coming weeks. The Intact announcement also appeared on insurance-canada.ca on October 23.

Intact's estimate is the larger. The company said third-quarter catastrophe losses were approximately C$660 million before tax, net of reinsurance, equal to $2.76 per diluted share after tax. Its release breaks the total down by geography: C$615 million in Canada, C$38 million in the UK and Ireland, and C$7 million in the United States. By line, personal property accounted for C$390 million, commercial lines C$173 million and personal auto C$52 million. Reinsurance News lists the three line items as summing to C$615 million, which matches the Canadian figure and not the C$660 million group total, because the UK and US losses are in addition. The company attributed the losses to severe storms causing flooding, water and wind damage across several regions, and to wildfires in British Columbia.

The estimate has an effect on Intact's full-year position. Its chief financial officer, Ken Anderson, said catastrophe losses for the trailing 12 months were C$1.29 billion, modestly above the company's annual guidance of C$1.20 billion. Management described 2025 and early 2026 as benign and noted that the third quarter is historically an active period for weather events. Chief executive Charles Brindamour said: "At an industry level, these events reinforce firm market conditions."

Definity's estimate is smaller but significant for a company of its size. It said catastrophe losses had an impact of approximately C$190 million on third-quarter underwriting income, net of reinsurance recoveries, equal to $1.15 per common share after tax and reinsurance. Personal property made up C$136 million, about 72% of the total, with C$37 million in commercial insurance and C$17 million in personal auto. Insurance Business describes the figure as an update to a preliminary estimate Definity issued on September 3 covering July and August, though the article does not give the earlier figure. Definity's president and chief executive, Rowan Saunders, said severe weather-related events over the summer continued into September and affected communities across the country.

The events behind the numbers are specific. Definity cited July and August severe rainstorms that caused flooding in Ontario and Alberta, wildfires in British Columbia and an early-September storm system that brought damaging winds, hail and flooding to southern Ontario. Insurance Business adds industry estimates from CatIQ, which tracks Canadian insured catastrophe losses: the June 30 to July 3 storms in southern Ontario and southern Quebec were estimated at C$491 million, much of it from basement flooding in Ottawa, and the Bald Range Fire near Summerland, British Columbia, at C$293 million. For comparison, industry-wide insured catastrophe losses were about C$2.4 billion in 2025, a quieter year, according to the article.

Two points stand out. First, water is driving claims at both carriers, and personal property is the largest line in each. Second, the loss figures are net of reinsurance, so they show what the insurers themselves bear after their reinsurance recoveries, and not the gross cost of the events to the industry. Neither announcement gave a combined ratio impact. Reinsurance News notes that the articles contain no prior-year comparison for either company, and Insurance Business reports no second-quarter catastrophe figures for either.

The implications for customers are mostly about pricing and terms. Insurance Business notes that some brokers had expected personal property pricing to ease, and that a quarter that pushed Intact above its catastrophe guidance makes that less likely, especially for flood-exposed urban homeowners. It also expects more focus on sewer backup and overland flood endorsements, deductibles and mitigation, especially in southwest Ottawa and parts of Alberta. That is the publication's assessment, not a statement from either insurer.

It helps to know what the headline figure means. An insurer's catastrophe loss estimate covers claims from events that the industry classes as catastrophes, and it is quoted after the insurer's reinsurance recoveries, so it shows the amount that hits the insurer's own results. It is also quoted before the full quarter's other items, such as ordinary claims, expenses and investment income, which is why a catastrophe estimate on its own does not tell shareholders what profit will be. The per-share figures, $2.76 for Intact and $1.15 for Definity, translate the after-tax effect into terms comparable with earnings per share, which is how analysts will adjust their forecasts. Readers should treat all of these as estimates. The full third-quarter reports will confirm the catastrophe figures, show how much of the loss was offset by reinsurance and give the combined ratios. Marsh's index for the third quarter, published October 21, recorded Canadian composite commercial rates down 6% on average, so the personal property pressure described here sits against a softer commercial market.
source_name: Insurance Business Canada (October 7, 2026), Reinsurance News (October 8, 2026) and insurance-canada.ca (October 23, 2026)
image_alt: Flooded residential street representing severe weather property claims (illustrative)
key_points: Intact Financial estimated third-quarter 2026 catastrophe losses of about C$660 million pre-tax, net of reinsurance, or $2.76 per diluted share after tax: C$615 million in Canada, C$38 million in the UK and Ireland and C$7 million in the US.

By line, Intact's losses were C$390 million personal property, C$173 million commercial lines and C$52 million personal auto; Intact's trailing 12-month catastrophe losses were C$1.29 billion, modestly above annual guidance of C$1.20 billion.

Definity Financial put the third-quarter impact on underwriting income at about C$190 million net of reinsurance recoveries, or $1.15 per common share: C$136 million personal property, C$37 million commercial and C$17 million personal auto.

Events cited include July and August rainstorms and flooding in Ontario and Alberta, wildfires in British Columbia and an early-September storm bringing wind, hail and flooding to southern Ontario; CatIQ put the June 30 to July 3 southern Ontario and Quebec storms at C$491 million and the Bald Range Fire near Summerland at C$293 million.

Intact chief executive Charles Brindamour said the events 'reinforce firm market conditions' at an industry level; industry insured catastrophe losses were about C$2.4 billion in 2025, a quieter year.
why_it_matters: Water damage from heavy rain and flooding is now a larger part of Canadian home insurance claims, and these estimates show how quickly a few storms can use up an insurer's annual allowance. For homeowners in flood-exposed cities such as Ottawa, the practical effects are on pricing and policy terms, since insurers cite firm market conditions and brokers are paying more attention to sewer backup and overland flood endorsements and deductibles. The estimates are preliminary and net of reinsurance, and full third-quarter results will give the combined ratios.

title: TAL, Owned by Japan's Dai-ichi Life, Bids A$11.80 a Share for Challenger, Australia's Largest Annuity Provider, in a Non-Binding Proposal Worth Nearly A$8 Billion
summary: TAL, the Australian life insurer owned by Japan's Dai-ichi Life, proposed on October 19, 2026 to buy the roughly 79.5% of Challenger it does not already own at A$11.80 a share, a 19.8% premium valuing Challenger at a little under A$8 billion; the proposal is non-binding and conditional on due diligence, approvals and a shareholder vote.
description:
A Japanese-owned insurer has made a proposal to buy Australia's largest annuity provider. On Monday, October 19, 2026, Challenger disclosed to the Australian Securities Exchange, alongside its first-quarter results for the 2027 financial year, that it had received a proposal from TAL, the Australian life insurer owned by Japan's Dai-ichi Life Group. According to Insurance Business, TAL offered A$11.80 per share for the roughly 79.5% of Challenger that it does not already hold.

The price represents a premium of 19.8% to Challenger's closing price of A$9.85 on the preceding Friday and 17.7% above the one-month volume-weighted average price of A$10.03. It values Challenger at a little under A$8 billion, and Insurance Business puts the cost of buying the shares TAL does not own at about A$6.3 billion. The proposal is not a firm offer. Challenger said: "The proposal is non-binding and conditional," and that its shareholders need take no action. Its board is considering the proposal, and a binding deal may not follow.

The conditions are the usual ones for a deal of this kind. TAL would need to complete due diligence and the two companies would have to agree a scheme implementation agreement. Regulatory approvals would be required, including likely sign-off from the Foreign Investment Review Board and the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority. Challenger's board would need to recommend the transaction, and because it would proceed as a scheme of arrangement, shareholders and the court would have to approve it. Any of these steps could change the price, the terms or the outcome.

The market's reaction suggests cautious optimism. Challenger's shares rose to A$11.41 on Monday, about 16% above Friday's close and the highest in eight years. The stock still traded below the A$11.80 offer, which Insurance Business reads as a sign that investors doubt the deal will complete, since the gap between the share price and the offer reflects the risk that it will fall through.

TAL is not approaching Challenger from a standing start. Insurance Business reports that it acquired MS&AD's 15.1% holding at about A$8.46 per share, a 53% premium to the prevailing price at the time, and then bought a further 4.8% from an Apollo-managed fund for about A$247 million, taking its holding to 19.9%. TAL's chief executive, Fiona Macgregor, described the investment as "an extension of our commitment to supporting Australians' financial needs during retirement." If the full transaction proceeds, Dai-ichi would own both Australia's largest protection insurer and its largest annuity provider.

Challenger's own performance gives context for the price. For the 2026 financial year, annuity sales rose 19% to A$6.2 billion and the annuity book grew 10.7%. In the first quarter of FY27, total sales rose 52% to A$4.4 billion. Fixed-term annuity sales more than doubled to A$2.2 billion, while lifetime annuity sales fell 2% to A$314 million. Assets under management rose 5% to A$31.9 billion, and offshore reinsurance sales rose 30% to A$320 million. Chief executive Nick Hamilton said sales momentum was strong across both domestic and offshore annuities. The article notes the timing relative to regulation: revised APRA capital rules for longevity products took effect on July 1, 2026.

Several issues remain open. Challenger's offshore business relies partly on its partnership with MS Primary, part of MS&AD, which has run since 2016. Insurance Business says it is unclear whether MS&AD would continue to send business to a company owned by a Japanese competitor. Challenger is also merging its Fidante funds business with Channel Capital and expects to keep 45% of the combined company, which a buyer would need to take into account.

Two terms are worth explaining. An annuity is a product that converts a lump sum, often from superannuation savings, into a regular income, either for a fixed term or for life, and the provider takes on the risk of customers living longer than expected. A scheme of arrangement is the court-supervised process by which a company can be acquired with the approval of a set majority of its shareholders, and it is why the timetable includes both a shareholder vote and a court hearing. The article does not give a timetable for either, and no date has been set for the board's response. For annuity holders, the practical position is that nothing changes now. Existing annuities are contracts with Challenger's life company, and a change of ownership would not by itself alter their terms, though the article does not discuss this. For shareholders, the decision will come only if the board recommends a binding scheme. For the market, the proposal is a sign of how much value investors and insurers attach to retirement income products as Australia's population ages. The headline premium of 19.8% is calculated against the pre-announcement close, and the one-month average comparison of 17.7% shows the offer is not far above recent trading. Readers should follow Challenger's ASX announcements for developments, as a non-binding proposal can be withdrawn or revised.
source_name: Insurance Business Australia (October 19, 2026) reporting TAL's proposal and Challenger's ASX announcement
image_alt: Business handshake representing a takeover proposal between insurers (illustrative)
key_points: TAL proposed A$11.80 per Challenger share for the roughly 79.5% it does not own, a 19.8% premium to the A$9.85 close before the announcement and 17.7% above the one-month volume-weighted average price of A$10.03, valuing Challenger at a little under A$8 billion.

The proposal is non-binding and conditional on due diligence, a scheme implementation agreement, regulatory approvals likely including FIRB and APRA, a board recommendation, and shareholder and court approval; Challenger said shareholders need take no action.

Challenger shares rose to A$11.41, about 16% above the prior close and their highest in eight years, but stayed below the offer price, which indicates the market is not certain the deal will complete.
TAL built its stake by buying MS&AD's 15.1% at about A$8.46 a share, a 53% premium to the price then, and a further 4.8% from an Apollo-managed fund for about A$247 million, reaching 19.9%.

Challenger reported first-quarter FY27 total sales up 52% to A$4.4 billion with assets under management of A$31.9 billion; if the deal proceeds, Dai-ichi would own both Australia's largest protection insurer and its largest annuity provider.
why_it_matters: Challenger is Australia's biggest provider of annuities, which turn a lump sum into a guaranteed income, and the retirement income market is growing as the population ages and regulators ease capital rules for longevity products. A takeover by an insurer that already leads in life protection would reshape that market. The proposal is only a first step: due diligence, regulators and Challenger's own shareholders all have to agree, and Challenger's reinsurance partnership with a Japanese competitor adds an open question. For existing annuitants, nothing changes unless a binding deal is completed.

title: French Supermarket Refrigeration Hack Hit About 700 Stores: Why Cyber Policies May Not Pay for Spoiled Food, and What Lockton Says to Check
summary: Attacks on internet-connected refrigeration controllers disrupted about 700 French supermarkets across Intermarché, Coopérative U and Carrefour in October 2026, with freezers reportedly reaching 40°C, and Lockton warns that cyber policies may exclude physical damage while property and stock-deterioration cover depends on policy wording.
description:
A cyberattack on supermarket refrigeration has given insurers and risk managers a concrete example of a loss that sits awkwardly between policies. Insurance Journal reported on October 21, 2026 that attacks on internet-connected refrigeration systems disrupted about 700 stores belonging to Intermarché, Coopérative U and Carrefour in France. The Groupement Mousquetaires, which owns Intermarché, said 300 of its stores were attacked, and Carrefour said 80 supermarkets were affected. No group has publicly claimed responsibility.

The mechanism is described in the report. The attackers targeted centralised fridge controllers that are connected to the internet so that contractors can monitor temperatures remotely. They gained access to some systems and changed settings, triggering prolonged defrost cycles that heated refrigerators and freezers. At an Intermarché store in Saint-Symphorien-le-Valois in Normandy, the store manager, Jérémy Béziaud, arrived to find freezers at 40°C and a fish cold-room ventilator at 70°C. "I threw out all the fresh food," he said. His store discarded about €3,000 of products and was running again the same day. Insurance Business Australia, in an article drawing on Lockton, reports that two supermarkets in Alsace recorded €270,000 in merchandise losses, without saying which stores.

The equipment manufacturer is named. Danfoss, a Danish company whose products were among those affected, said most of the compromised devices were obsolete models and that they "no longer received software or security updates." Mousquetaires said its refrigeration supplier is responsible for cleaning up its systems. Experts quoted by Insurance Journal said retail equipment is often 10 to 15 years old and was installed when cyber threats were less prominent, and that remote maintenance and software updates can expose equipment that was traditionally separate from corporate IT networks. No total loss figure has been published. Intermarché's chief executive warned that nationwide losses could reach tens of millions of euros in a single day. For comparison, Insurance Journal cites the 2025 attacks on the UK retailers Co-op, with a sales hit of more than £200 million, and Marks & Spencer, with an estimated £300 million fall in operating profit and online services disrupted for four months.

Lockton's analysis addresses the insurance question. Mark Luckin, national manager for cyber and technology, and Andrew Curl, head of corporate in Queensland, both at Lockton Australia, argue that cyberattacks can cause financial losses well beyond data breaches and ransomware. Businesses with large physical assets, perishable inventory or complex supply chains should check how their policies would respond, they say, "particularly when financial losses continue after affected systems have been restored." Their points about cover are these. Traditional cyber policies typically cover incident response, system restoration and some business interruption, but may exclude physical damage. Property policies generally respond to insured physical damage but can contain exclusions or restrictions for cyber events. Deterioration of stock insurance is available in Australia, but whether it responds to a cyber-induced refrigeration failure depends on the wording. Specialist cyber-physical damage cover can fill the gaps, and the article points to Aon's analysis of such products. Some cyber policies also include contingent business interruption for third-party disruptions, but protection depends on circumstances and terms.

The other losses that follow an incident are listed as emergency response costs, additional logistics costs, lost revenue and the cost of restoring normal operations. The article notes that these can accumulate after the initial disruption is contained, which makes the final impact hard to measure quickly. It also says manufacturers, warehouse operators and logistics providers rely on connected systems in the same way, and points to Australia's operational technology cyber security guidance on supply chain and industrial system protection.

What the sources do not say is as important. No insurer has been quoted on how it would treat these French losses, and the claim that French supermarkets' cyber insurance is unlikely to cover food losses is a headline on a related Insurance Journal article whose text was not available for this report. It would be a mistake to conclude that no cover will respond. Coverage turns on each retailer's policies, which are not public, and on whether the cause is treated as cyber or physical.

Other experts quoted make the broader point. Harjinder Singh Lallie of the University of Warwick said retail is targeted "because they're weak and it can have a massive impact on society." Laura Duncan of PwC asked whether businesses could "do things manually with pen and paper," and Luca Berni of Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 said retailers "depend on vast networks of interconnected technologies." Experts also warned that AI could help attackers find weaknesses and write convincing phishing messages.

For businesses, the practical steps follow from the coverage: list equipment that is connected to the internet, find out whether it still receives security updates, ask the broker in writing which policy would respond to a cyber-caused spoilage loss, and plan for operating manually during an outage.
source_name: Insurance Journal (October 21, 2026) and Insurance Business Australia, reporting Lockton Australia analysis (October 20, 2026)
image_alt: Padlock over digital circuitry representing a cyberattack on connected equipment (illustrative)
key_points: Attacks on centralised, internet-connected fridge controllers disrupted about 700 stores across Intermarché, Coopérative U and Carrefour; Groupement Mousquetaires said 300 of its stores were attacked and Carrefour said 80 supermarkets were affected, and no group has claimed responsibility.

Attackers changed settings to trigger prolonged defrost cycles; at one Normandy Intermarché freezers reportedly reached 40°C and a fish cold-room ventilator 70°C, and the store threw out about €3,000 of products; two Alsace supermarkets reported €270,000 in merchandise losses.

Danfoss said most compromised devices were obsolete models that 'no longer received software or security updates'; Intermarché's chief executive warned nationwide losses could reach tens of millions of euros in a single day, but no total loss figure has been published.

Lockton Australia says traditional cyber policies may exclude physical damage, property policies can restrict cyber events, and stock deterioration cover depends on its wording, so businesses with perishable inventory should check how their cover would respond.

A related Insurance Journal headline says French supermarkets' cyber insurance is unlikely to cover food losses, but its text was not available for this article; no insurer has commented in the sources reviewed.
why_it_matters: Most people think of cyberattacks as stolen data or locked computers. This case shows an attack on the equipment that keeps food cold, where the loss is spoiled stock and lost sales, not just data. That kind of loss can fall between insurance policies: a cyber policy may exclude physical damage, while a property policy may exclude cyber causes. For any business with refrigeration, manufacturing lines or building controls connected to the internet, the lesson from the coverage is to ask the broker, before a loss, which policy would respond and whether old equipment still receives security updates.

title: AM Best: Commercial Auto Liability Lost $6.4 Billion in 2024 as Litigation Costs Outpace 14 Straight Years of Rate Increases
summary: An AM Best special report on social inflation, reported on October 19, 2026, says first-year commercial auto liability loss payments grew 6.4% a year from 2014 to 2024, more than double economic inflation, leaving the line with a $4.9 billion underwriting loss in 2024 and an estimated $4 billion to $5 billion reserve shortfall despite 14 consecutive years of rate increases.
description:
Commercial auto liability remains one of the least profitable lines in US property and casualty insurance, and a new AM Best special report quantifies how far claim costs are outrunning prices. Insurance Business reported on October 19, 2026 that the rating agency's report on the effect of social inflation on US liability results finds that litigation, not ordinary economic inflation, is the main driver of the gap.

The headline comparison is between claims and inflation. According to the report, first-year commercial auto liability loss payments grew at 6.4% a year from 2014 to 2024. That is more than double the 2.8% average economic inflation rate over the period. A September 2025 AM Best review put severity, the average cost per claim, at growth of about 8% annually over the past nine years. Insurers have responded with 14 consecutive years of rate increases, mostly in the upper single digits to double digits, but the article says premiums have not closed the gap.

The underwriting results show the consequence. The overall commercial auto line posted a $4.9 billion underwriting loss in 2024. Commercial auto liability alone accounted for a $6.4 billion loss, which was partly offset by a $1.5 billion profit in physical damage, the part of the line that covers damage to the insured's own vehicles. Among the 20 largest commercial auto insurers, 14 posted combined ratios above 100 in 2024, meaning their claims and expenses exceeded premiums, and 14 had underwriting losses in at least three of the past five years. The article does not give a combined ratio specific to commercial auto liability.

Reserves are a second concern. AM Best estimates that the line is under-reserved by $4 billion to $5 billion industry-wide. Under-reserving means insurers have set aside less money for claims already incurred than the claims are likely to cost, and when that is recognised, it reduces profit. David Blades of AM Best describes adverse loss development as "a constant drain on commercial auto results and is getting worse." Christopher Graham of AM Best said: "Legal system abuse comes in several forms and can have a severe impact on insurers' results."

The report points to nuclear verdicts, defined as jury awards of $10 million or more, as a defining feature of commercial auto liability claims, though the article gives no count or dollar total. It cites other data on the legal environment. Swiss Re found that annual liability claim costs peaked near 7% in 2023, a 20-year high. Third-party litigation funding, in which outside investors finance lawsuits in return for a share of any award, is a market estimated at $17 billion, of which the United States accounts for about 52%, according to Swiss Re.

Some reforms show an effect. The article cites Florida's HB 837, after which auto glass lawsuits fell from 24,720 in the second quarter of 2023 to 2,613 in the second quarter of 2024, according to Milliman. That is one example of how a change in law can reduce litigation, though it concerns glass claims and not the large injury claims that drive commercial auto liability losses.

The buying side has also changed. The article cites WTW data from 2023 that 55% of large, complex clients bought umbrella and primary liability cover from the same carrier, up from 37% in 2015, and that average umbrella limits for those structures fell to $11.2 million from $20.1 million. Lower limits mean the insurer pays less when a large verdict comes, and the business keeps more risk or must buy additional layers elsewhere. The data are from 2023 and the article does not say how much they have changed since.

For insurers, the implications are about discipline. The report suggests that rate increases alone have not been enough, which means insurers must also be selective about the fleets they write, raise attachment points and manage claims more actively. For fleet operators, it means continued pressure on premiums and terms,. Marsh's third-quarter index, published October 21, shows US casualty rates rising 6% in the quarter, which is consistent with the pressure AM Best describes.

Social inflation is the term insurers use for claim costs rising faster than general inflation because of changes in the legal and social environment, such as larger jury awards, wider theories of liability, litigation funding and attorney advertising. The term covers developments that raise the cost of settling injury claims after the accident itself has happened. It is not a single measurable item, which is why reports like this compare claims growth with economic inflation to estimate its size. The 6.4% annual growth in loss payments against 2.8% economic inflation is one such comparison, and it implies that the gap compounds over a decade. The figures come from AM Best's report as summarised by Insurance Business, and the original report should be consulted for definitions, the full dataset and the methodology behind the reserve estimate.
source_name: Insurance Business US (October 19, 2026) reporting an AM Best special report on social inflation
image_alt: Commercial trucks on a highway representing commercial auto liability exposure (illustrative)
key_points: First-year commercial auto liability loss payments grew 6.4% a year from 2014 to 2024, more than double the 2.8% average economic inflation rate; severity has grown about 8% annually over nine years, according to a September 2025 AM Best review.
The commercial auto line posted a $4.9 billion underwriting loss in 2024: commercial auto liability lost $6.4 billion, partly offset by a $1.5 billion profit in physical damage.

Among the top 20 commercial auto insurers, 14 posted combined ratios above 100 in 2024, and 14 had underwriting losses in at least three of the past five years, despite 14 consecutive years of rate increases mostly in the upper single to double digits.

AM Best estimates the line is under-reserved by $4 billion to $5 billion industry-wide, and David Blades describes adverse loss development as 'a constant drain on commercial auto results and is getting worse'.

Jury awards of $10 million or more, known as nuclear verdicts, are described as a defining feature of US commercial auto liability claims; Swiss Re data in the report show US liability claim costs peaked near 7% growth in 2023, a 20-year high.
why_it_matters: Commercial auto liability covers the damage and injuries a business's vehicles cause to others, and it pays for trucks, delivery vans and contractor fleets. When the cost of claims keeps rising faster than prices, insurers can leave the line or push rates higher, which affects any business that runs vehicles. The AM Best figures show the gap is large even after 14 years of price rises, and that reserves for past claims may be too low, which can lead to further rate increases. For consumers, the effect shows up indirectly in the cost of goods and services that depend on commercial fleets.

title: Marsh Global Insurance Market Index: Commercial Rates Fall 5% in Q3 2026, the Ninth Straight Decline, as US Casualty Rises 6% and Pacific and IMEA Drop 12% and 14%
summary: Marsh's Global Insurance Market Index, published October 21, 2026, shows global commercial insurance rates down 5% in the third quarter after a 6% fall in the second, led by a 10% drop in property and offset by a 1% rise in casualty, with regional falls from 1% in the US to 14% in India, the Middle East and Africa.
description:
Businesses buying insurance continued to benefit from falling prices in the third quarter of 2026, with one important exception. Marsh's Global Insurance Market Index, published on October 21, 2026, shows that global commercial insurance rates fell an average of 5% in the quarter. That followed a 6% decline in the second quarter, and it is the ninth straight quarterly decrease, as reported by Insurance Journal and in Marsh's own release.

The pattern by line is uneven. Property was the biggest driver of the decline, with rates down 10% globally. Marsh's figures show that property fell 9% in the first quarter and 12% in the second, so the third-quarter fall is smaller than the second but still large. By region, property fell most in India, the Middle East and Africa, at 15%, followed by the Pacific at 14% and Latin America and the Caribbean at 13%. The UK saw an 11% fall, the US 10%, Europe 9%, Canada 8% and Asia 7%. Casualty was the only line that rose, up 1% globally after a 2% increase in the second quarter. The increase was driven by the United States, where casualty rates rose 6% after rising 7% in the previous quarter, and every other region recorded a decrease. Insurance Journal reports that litigation and large settlements affected US pricing, and that capacity became more selective, with higher attachment points.

Financial and professional lines fell 3% globally, the 17th consecutive quarterly decline, although US rates in this category rose 1%. Cyber rates fell 4% globally, the 13th straight quarterly decline, but in the US they were flat, which ended that country's run of decreases. The release does not give a separate rate figure for directors and officers liability, but says insurers focused on that line and that double-digit reductions were achieved in select situations.

The regional composites show how widely the softening is spread. The US composite fell 1%, after a 2% fall in the second quarter, so it is the market closest to stability. Canada fell 6%, the UK 8%, Europe 6% and Asia 6%. Latin America and the Caribbean fell 9%, the Pacific 12%, and India, the Middle East and Africa, reported together, fell 14%.

Marsh's explanation is that strong insurer financial results, favourable reinsurance terms, new market entrants and expanded capacity from managing general agents have all contributed. John Donnelly, president of global placement at Marsh, said: "Market conditions remained broadly unchanged, with continued rate pressure across much of the market," and, according to Insurance Journal, that a benign US hurricane season contributed to favourable underwriting results. Buyers have generally obtained lower rates, broader coverage, higher limits, lower deductibles and long-term agreements. Some used the savings to restructure programmes, add limits or broaden coverage, but Donnelly noted that many buyers were "more inclined to retain premium savings rather than reinvesting them in additional coverage," against an uncertain geopolitical backdrop.

The index also lists where underwriters are still cautious: catastrophe exposure, US casualty, directors and officers liability, and cyber risks tied to artificial intelligence, vendor dependencies, privacy and ransomware. Marsh observed that early signs of rate stabilisation emerged in the third quarter, a cautious statement that falls short of predicting an end to the decline.

Other data published this month are consistent with the picture. Munich Re raised its profit target on October 23 after light major losses, while telling investors that its July renewals saw volume and prices fall. Gallagher Re said global insured catastrophe losses for the first nine months of 2026 were the lowest since 2019. Selective Insurance, in its third-quarter results, reported an average renewal price increase of 5.6% but a 7% fall in written premium as it pruned weaker business. Together they describe a market in which prices are lower for many buyers but insurers are trying to protect margins by being selective.

Two terms help in reading the index. A composite rate is the average change in the price of renewing programmes across all lines in a region, so a 5% fall means a typical programme cost about 5% less than a year earlier for the same exposure. Attachment points are the level of loss at which an insurance layer begins to pay, and raising them shifts more of a loss to the buyer or to lower layers of cover. Both ideas explain why a buyer can see a lower premium and still carry more of the risk. What the index does not show is the experience of any one buyer. It measures the change in price on renewing programmes, weighted across a large sample, and does not account for changes in cover, so an individual company's renewal may differ widely depending on its loss record, industry, location and the lines it buys. For readers who want precise definitions, the release and the full index data are available from Marsh.
source_name: Marsh Global Insurance Market Index press release (October 21, 2026) and Insurance Journal (October 21, 2026)
image_alt: Charts and analytics dashboard representing insurance market pricing data (illustrative)
key_points: Marsh's global composite commercial insurance rate fell 5% in the third quarter of 2026, after a 6% decline in the second quarter, the ninth straight quarterly decrease.
Property rates fell 10% globally (12% in Q2 and 9% in Q1), while casualty was the only line to rise, up 1%, with US casualty up 6% (7% in Q2) and every other region lower.
Regional composites: US -1% (from -2%), Canada -6%, UK -8%, Europe -6%, Asia -6%, Latin America and Caribbean -9%, Pacific -12% and India, Middle East and Africa -14%.
Financial and professional lines fell 3% globally, the 17th consecutive quarterly decline, and cyber fell 4%, the 13th straight decline, though US cyber rates were flat.

John Donnelly of Marsh said market conditions 'remained broadly unchanged' and that many buyers were 'more inclined to retain premium savings rather than reinvesting them in additional coverage'; Marsh noted early signs of rate stabilisation in Q3.
why_it_matters: The Marsh index is one of the most widely cited measures of what businesses pay for commercial insurance. Nine straight quarterly falls mean that many companies are renewing at lower prices, with broader cover, higher limits or lower deductibles in some cases. The split matters: property is getting cheaper after a quiet catastrophe year and plentiful capacity, while US casualty, which is affected by litigation costs, is still rising. For buyers, this is a period to negotiate; for insurers, falling rates put pressure on margins.
